title: Sprint summit: three peaks and a monster
summary: Take the 21 game to the family and present its proof, then climb three peaks over exponents, fraction division and the number map, and settle the month 1 monster.

steps.title: The climb, in order
steps.body:
Today has three parts, in this order: warm up your 21 game, run the family gauntlet, then climb the summit.

Before the family gauntlet, go back to the take-away game you invented in week three. Bring your own maximum, your own starting pile, and your own safe piles. Present it to your family: state your rule and starting pile out loud. Give them a minute to find a safe pile, then show your proof. Name the idea out loud as you explain it, domino proof, not just 'I did this'. Show the first domino, the repeating step, and say whether your own starting pile is safe for whoever moves first. Teach it well enough that they could invent their own take-away game.

The summit has three peaks, one for each week of the sprint: fast forward, how many fit, and the number map. Each peak ends in one Summit problem built to be harder than the rest. If a Summit problem slows you down, that is the mountain doing its job. Slow on purpose beats fast and wrong on every summit in the world.

Keep the counters within reach: after the warm-up you take the 21 game to the family, and after the climb one old monster is waiting for its ending.

problems.prompt: In the 21 game you may take 1, 2 or 3 counters, and whoever takes the last counter wins. A parent hands you a pile of 18. How many counters do you take right now?
explanation: The piles you want to hand your opponent are the multiples of 4, the doomed piles. From one of those, whatever they take, you can bring the pile down to the next doomed pile, all the way to zero.
18 is not a multiple of 4. The nearest multiple of 4 below it is 16.
Take 2, leaving a pile of 16 counters. From then on, whatever they take, you take enough to make your two takes add up to 4 together. The last counter is yours.
problems.useAgain: when a game lets you plan backwards from the end, so you can hand your opponent a doomed spot on purpose.
hints: Which piles would you hate to be handed? Work backwards from the smallest piles and mark the doomed ones.
Find the biggest doomed pile that is smaller than 18, and get the pile there.
problems.socraticHint: Suppose you could hand your opponent a doomed pile. What could you then do after every move they make?

variant.prompt: Same 21 game: a grandparent hands you a pile of 15. How many counters do you take right now?

problems.prompt: It is your turn in the 21 game and 12 counters are left. True or false: if the other player knows the winning positions, they will win no matter how well you play.
explanation: 12 is a multiple of 4, and the player standing on a multiple of 4 is the one in trouble.
Take 1, 2 or 3 and the pile lands between 9 and 11 counters. From there your opponent can always bring it back to 8, then to 4, then to 0.
Whoever brings the pile to 0 took the last counter, so the trap closes on you three moves ahead of time.
problems.useAgain: when you want to know whether a game position is already decided before another move is even made.
hints: Check whether 12 is one of the doomed piles you mapped in week 1.
Try all three of your possible takes. After each one, what can your opponent do to the pile?
problems.socraticHint: Is there any take from 12 that does not let your opponent land the pile right back on a multiple of 4?

variant.prompt: It is your turn in the 21 game and 13 counters are left. True or false: playing right, you can win from here every single time.

steps.title: Present the 21 game and its proof
steps.prompt: Gather the family and the counters. Teach the 21 game in two sentences, then take on all comers: any pile size they choose, you name your move without counting on your fingers. When the table is beaten, present the proof out loud like a mathematician: the first domino, why a pile of 4 is doomed for whoever faces it, then the repeating knock, why every pile 4 bigger stays doomed. Finish with what this makes 21: one step away from doom, which is exactly why going first wins.

problems.prompt: Peak 1, fast forward: your week 1 board had 2 buttons and could show 4 different on-off patterns. A control panel has 6 switches, each one on or off. How many different patterns can the panel show?
explanation: Each switch is its own on-or-off choice, so every extra switch doubles the number of patterns.
One switch gives 2 patterns. Two switches give 2 x 2, which is 4, exactly what your two buttons showed.
Six switches give 2 multiplied by itself six times, which is 2 to the power 6.
Doubling from 2: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. The panel can show 64 patterns.
problems.useAgain: when the same doubling repeats over and over and a power gets you the total without stepping through every stage.
hints: Start tiny: count the patterns for 1 switch, then 2, then 3, and watch what each extra switch does to the total.
Each extra switch doubles the total, and you double once per switch.
problems.socraticHint: Why does adding one switch double the number of patterns instead of just adding a few more?

variant.prompt: A control panel has 7 switches, each one on or off. How many different patterns can it show?

problems.prompt: One of these is an impostor: it does not equal 2 to the power 4. Which one?
explanation: 2 to the power 4 means multiply four 2s together: 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 is 16.
4 to the power 2 is 4 x 4, which is also 16, and 8 x 2 is 16 as well.
2 + 2 + 2 + 2 is repeated adding, not repeated multiplying: it makes 8.
An exponent is a fast forward button for multiplication, never for addition, so the adding one is the impostor.
problems.useAgain: when an expression dresses up like a power and you need to check whether it really multiplies.
hints: Work each option out to a plain number first.
Three of the options land on the same number.
problems.socraticHint: What is the difference between four 2s added together and four 2s multiplied together?

variant.prompt: One of these is an impostor: it does not equal 3 to the power 3. Which one?

problems.prompt: Peak 1 keeps climbing, money version: you put 100 dollars in the family bank. It pays 10 percent interest every year, and the interest stays in the bank to earn interest of its own. How much is in the bank after 2 years?
explanation: Year one: 10 percent of 100 dollars is 10 dollars, so the bank ends the year holding 110.00.
Year two starts from 110, not from the original 100. 10 percent of 110 is 11 dollars.
110 plus 11 is 121.00. The extra dollar is the snowball: last year's interest earned interest of its own.
This is doubling's slower cousin: the same growth rule applied again and again, which is exactly what an exponent fast forwards.
problems.useAgain: when money or anything else grows by the same percent each round, and the new growth rides on top of the old.
hints: Work one year at a time, and write down the new total after year one.
In year two, take 10 percent of the year one total, not of the 100 you started with.
problems.socraticHint: Why is year two's interest bigger than year one's, when the percent never changed?

variant.prompt: You put 200 dollars in the family bank. It pays 10 percent interest every year, and the interest stays in to earn its own. How much is in the bank after 2 years?

problems.prompt: Summit: a mystery panel of on-off switches shows exactly 32 different patterns. The builder adds 2 more switches. How many patterns can it show now?
explanation: First run the fast forward backwards: how many doublings from 1 reach 32? Count them: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 is five doublings, so the panel has 5 switches.
Adding 2 switches makes 7 switches, and each one doubles the total like every switch does.
32 doubled is 64, and 64 doubled is 128. Seven switches show 128 patterns, which is 2 to the power 7.
problems.useAgain: when a power problem hands you the total and hides the exponent, so you count the doublings backwards first.
hints: Before touching the new switches, work out how many switches make exactly 32 patterns.
Then let each added switch do to the total what every switch does.
problems.socraticHint: Could a panel of on-off switches ever show exactly 40 patterns? What does your answer tell you about the number 32?

variant.prompt: A mystery panel of on-off switches shows exactly 8 different patterns. The builder adds 2 more switches. How many patterns can it show now?

problems.prompt: Peak 2, how many fit: a jug holds 1 1/2 cups of milk. Your scoop holds 1/4 cup. How many scoops does it take to empty the jug?
explanation: Dividing by 1/4 asks: how many quarter cups fit inside 1 1/2 cups?
Each whole cup holds 4 quarters, so the first cup gives 4 scoops.
The extra 1/2 cup holds 2 quarters, so 2 more scoops.
4 plus 2 is 6 scoops. The flip rule agrees: 3/2 x 4 is 12/2, which is 6.
problems.useAgain: when dividing by a fraction turns into the question of how many small pieces fit inside the big amount.
hints: Ask first: how many quarter cups fit in one whole cup?
Then count the quarters hiding in the extra half cup.
problems.socraticHint: Why does dividing by a fraction smaller than 1 give an answer bigger than the amount you started with?

variant.prompt: A jug holds 2 1/2 cups of milk. Your scoop holds 1/4 cup. How many scoops does it take to empty the jug?

problems.prompt: Before computing anything, one of these divisions lands bigger than 1. Which one?
explanation: Division asks how many of the second number fit inside the first.
If the first number is bigger than the second, more than one fits, so the answer beats 1 every time. If the first is smaller, less than one whole fits.
Only in 3/4 divided by 1/2 is the first fraction the bigger one: 3/4 beats 1/2.
The flip rule confirms it: 3/4 x 2 is 6/4, which is 1 1/2, bigger than 1.
problems.useAgain: when you can size up a division's answer before doing any arithmetic, just by comparing the two amounts.
hints: For each pair, decide: is the first fraction bigger or smaller than the second?
When something smaller is measured out of something bigger, does it fit more than once or less than once?
problems.socraticHint: Without computing anything, what would have to be true about the two fractions for the answer to land exactly on 1?

variant.prompt: Before computing anything, one of these divisions lands bigger than 1. Which one?

problems.prompt: Summit: a ribbon is 3 1/2 meters long. Each bow needs 3/4 of a meter of ribbon. How many whole bows can you cut?
explanation: How many fit: 3 1/2 divided by 3/4. Flip and multiply: 7/2 x 4/3 is 28/6, which is 4 and 2/3.
So 3/4 of a meter fits into the ribbon 4 whole times, with 2/3 of a bow's worth of ribbon left over.
Two thirds of a bow is not a bow. You can cut 4 whole bows.
Check the leftover: 4 bows use 3 meters, leaving 1/2 a meter, and 1/2 is less than the 3/4 a fifth bow needs.
problems.useAgain: when a division answer has a fraction part but the real question only counts whole pieces.
hints: First find how many times 3/4 fits into 3 1/2, fraction part and all.
Then decide what a fraction of a bow is worth in real life.
problems.socraticHint: Your division lands between two whole numbers. Which neighbour does the ribbon question actually want, and why?

variant.prompt: A rope is 5 1/2 meters long. Each swing seat needs 3/4 of a meter of rope. How many whole seats can you cut?

problems.prompt: Peak 3, the number map: the point (-3, 5) sits 3 steps left of zero and 5 steps up. Which quarter of the coordinate plane holds it?
explanation: The coordinate plane is two number lines crossed. The first number is your step on the left and right line, and negative means left of zero.
The second number is your step on the up and down line, and positive means up.
Left and up together put the point in the top left quarter, which is quadrant 2.
problems.useAgain: when a point's two signs, read off the two number lines, are enough to place it before you plot a single square.
hints: The first number moves you across. Which direction is negative across?
The second number moves you up or down. Which direction is positive?
problems.socraticHint: Which quadrant would (3, 5) land in, and what did flipping that one sign do to the spot?

variant.prompt: The point (4, -2) sits 4 steps right of zero and 2 steps down. Which quarter of the coordinate plane holds it?

explanation: Multiply before you add, so (-3) x 4 goes first.
On the number line, (-3) x 4 is four jumps of 3 to the left of zero, landing on -12.
Then add 5: from -12, walk 5 steps to the right, landing on -7.
problems.useAgain: when signs get confusing and walking the number line settles which side of zero you end on.
hints: Order of operations still rules here: which part happens first?
Walk it on a number line: where do four jumps of 3 to the left leave you?
problems.socraticHint: Before computing: the multiply pulls the answer left of zero and the add pushes it right. Which pull is stronger here?

problems.prompt: Summit: a rectangle's corners sit at (-2, 1), (4, 1), (4, -3) and (-2, -3). Sketch it on graph paper if that helps. What is the rectangle's perimeter?
explanation: The top side runs from (-2, 1) to (4, 1). From 2 steps left of zero to 4 steps right of zero is 2 plus 4, which is 6 steps across.
The right side runs from (4, 1) down to (4, -3). From 1 step up to 3 steps down is 1 plus 3, which is 4 steps.
A rectangle uses each side length twice: 6 plus 4 is 10, and twice 10 is 20.
Crossing zero is the whole trick: a side that crosses zero adds its distances on the two sides of zero instead of subtracting them.
problems.useAgain: when corner coordinates hide a shape's real side lengths, and reading each side off its number line sets them free.
hints: Find the length of the top side first: how far is it from -2 across to 4?
A distance that crosses zero adds the distance on each side of zero.
problems.socraticHint: The top side starts left of zero and ends right of zero. What does crossing zero do to how you measure its length?

variant.prompt: A rectangle's corners sit at (-3, 1), (2, 1), (2, -2) and (-3, -2). What is the rectangle's perimeter?

problems.prompt: The month 1 monster gets its ending today, cracked or retired with honours: the 1-2-4 game. A pile starts with 20 counters. On your turn you take 1, 2 or 4 counters, and whoever takes the last counter wins. You move first. Can you always win, and what is your complete plan? Crack it the way you cracked 21: work backwards and label the doomed piles.

mustMention: the doomed piles are the multiples of 3

explanation: Work backwards. With 1, 2 or 4 counters left on your turn, you take them all and win. With 3 left, you can only take 1 or 2, leaving 2 or 1, and the other player scoops the rest: 3 is doomed.

A pile is safe for you when some move hands your opponent a doomed pile. From a pile of 4, taking 1 hands them a doomed pile. From 5, taking 2 does the same. From 6, your takes leave 5, 4 or 2, and none of those is doomed, so 6 is doomed too.
Keep climbing and the doomed piles land on 3, 6, 9, 12: the multiples of 3, every single one. From any other pile you can always step onto a multiple of 3, and from a multiple of 3 you never can.

Now the sneaky part: taking 4 never opens a single new door. Taking 4 and taking 1 leave the pile the same distance from the multiples of 3 below it. The flashy extra move is a costume on take 1, and this is secretly the take 1 or 2 game.

20 is not a multiple of 3, so you can always win. Take 2 to leave 18, then after every move of theirs bring the pile back to a multiple of 3 again. They take 1, you take 2; they take 2, you take 1; they take 4, you take 2, and the last counter is yours.
problems.useAgain: when a new game looks bigger and scarier than one you have already beaten, and backward labels reveal it is the old game in a costume.
hints: Play it small first: start from piles of 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, and mark which starting piles you would hate to be handed.
In the 21 game the doomed piles climbed by 4 because the takes were 1, 2 and 3. Watch what the doomed piles climb by here.
problems.socraticHint: Compare taking 4 with taking 1. What does each one do to the pile's distance from the nearest doomed pile below it?

variant.prompt: Same moves, new game: the pile starts with 24 counters, and this time you may choose whether to go first or second. Which do you choose, and what is your plan to win every time?

mustMention: after each of their moves, bring the pile back to a multiple of 3

steps.title: Explain it
steps.prompt: Write the crack of the 1-2-4 monster for a friend who has only ever played the 21 game: one idea per sentence, working backwards and the winning positions both named out loud. Finish with the single sentence that unmasks the take 4 move.
